extraction.body: Amazon has steadily improved its lineup of Fire tablets since 2022. But specs are only part of the equation. Without better software, these slates are as good as useless. Getting the Play Store on your Fire Tablet opens the door to millions more apps. This guide walks you through installing Google's app store on your device, with instructions for models dating to 2014, up to and including the latest Fire tablets. Our guide also cites some common problems and how to fix them. We updated and verified that this process works using a Fire tablet that runs Fire OS 8.3.3.4. Amazon's Fire tablets run on Fire OS, a forked version of the Android operating system. Because the core software is Android, substituting or replacing the Amazon App Store with the Play Store, complete with all the Google apps you won't find elsewhere, is a cinch. Whether you're looking for YouTube, Chrome, Gmail, or other apps that haven't made it to Amazon's app marketplace, this is an essential step for anyone with a Fire device. Before starting, you must download and activate the apps you want to install from outside the Amazon Appstore. This step allows you to open and install applications from downloaded APK files, which is how you'll get the Play Store running. Only download apps from trusted sources, as sideloading is an easy way to subject yourself to vulnerabilities. We recommend installing these apps from APK Mirror, a trusted source for APKs across the web. On older models running legacy software, activating Apps from Unknown Sources might be a single toggle, not a per-app choice. This removes the third step above. Turn on the permission in step two to continue. Now, you're ready to download and install the APKs needed to run the Google Play Store. The next step is to download the proper APK files for the Google Play Store. These are Google Account Manager, Google Services Framework, Google Play Services, and Google Play Store. The first three apps handle basic account services and add APIs, while the last app is the app store. Who needs Google Play when you have APKMirror? Because different Fire tablets run different versions of Android with varying hardware (ranging from Android 5 to Android 11), the exact APKs you will install depend on the Fire tablet model. If you're unsure which model you have, figuring it out is easy. You're halfway done. For these last two applications, click the link for your device, then select the version closest to the top of the list that doesn't have "beta" in the name. Again, don't open the files and ignore messages about newer versions being available. When selecting the Google Play Store APK, ensure you choose the correct version that works with the latest version of Fire OS; we use Android 10+ for the Fire Max 11 (since Fire OS 8 is based on Android 11). Note that the process may take a few minutes. Fire models from 2022 and later (including the Fire 7, HD 8, HD 10, and Max 11) Google Play Services (64-bit ARM, nodpi, Android 11+) Google Play Services (64-bit ARM, nodpi, Android 9.0+) Google Play Services (32-bit ARM, nodpi, Android 6.0+) Google Play Services (64-bit ARM, nodpi, Android 6.0+) Fire HD 10 (7th Gen and older), Fire HD 8 (7th Gen and older), Fire 7 (7th Gen and older), Fire HD 6, Fire HDX 8.9 Google Play Services (32-bit ARM, nodpi, Android 5.0+) After downloading the four apps, it's time to install them. Amazon updated its Fire lineup with two new tablets in 2022: the Amazon Fire 7 and the Amazon Fire HD 8 . These devices feature improved performance, new colors, and, in the case of the Fire 7, USB-C charging for the first time. However, installing the Google Play Store seems to be an issue. At launch, neither device seemed capable of running the Play Store, even when following the directions in this guide. This concerned us, but it looks as though whatever issues were here are now fixed. When we updated this guide in May 2023, the most recent version of Fire OS for these two devices was Fire OS 8.3.1.8. We factory reset the Fire 7 and re-performed the steps above, and everything is still working as expected. If you have trouble, make sure your tablet is up to date. It could be the difference between accessing the Play Store after 15 minutes and spending an afternoon with non-stop headaches. If you get the error "This account already exists on your device" when signing in to Chrome or another Google app, or if the app doesn't detect your Google account, follow these steps: If you can't sign in to the Play Store, clear the app's local data. This resets the Play Store app to its original state and should fix most problems. If that didn't help, follow the above steps again, but restart your tablet before opening the Play Store. If that doesn't work, force-stop and clear data for Google Play Services and the Play Store. If you still can't get the Play Store to work, your best option is to factory reset your tablet and try again. Make sure you don't restore from a backup when setting up the tablet unless you made the backup before you installed the Play Store. sources.title: Kids Space is Google's new kid-friendly mode for Android tablets - Pocket-lint
passages: It's a new mode for Android tablets that's entirely kid-friendly and complete with parental controls.
Arriving first on Lenovo’s new Tab M10 HD Gen 2, Kids Space will come to more devices in the future.

Lenovo noted, however, that tablets in families are usually shared among many household members, so having a normal tablet that can enter a kids' mode is perhaps more useful than a kids' tablet itself.
Kids Space is separate from Google’s Family Link, a parental control app for Android devices that lets you set limits on screen time.
“Join us in our journey as we continue to create productive and healthy experiences for kids that adapt to the evolving world and needs of your family,” Google said in a blog.

With Kids Space, which is meant for kids under age nine, children can easily navigate a colourful interface to access a safe library of apps, games, videos, and books, which Google described as “enriching, high-quality, and trustworthy" content.
Elyse Betters Picaro is the former Editor-in-Chief of Pocket-lint and the former Operations Manager for Valnet's Consumer Tech brands, including Pocket-lint, Android Police, and XDA.
Kinds can create an avatar for themselves, too, while parents can add additional apps through the Google Play Store.

passages: Handing your child a tablet with unlimited access to apps, games, and the internet at large is not a good idea.
However, tablets can be great for kids if used with safeguards in place.
That's what both Amazon Kids and Google Kids Space aim to provide, but they do it very differently.
The story on device compatibility is pretty straightforward.
Amazon Kids is available on Amazon Fire tablets, and you don't actually need a special Kids model to use it.
You can also attempt to install the app yourself .
They both have the same goal in mind: to provide a safe and easy-to-use tablet interface for kids.
How they do this is pretty different on the surface, but that core principle is the same.

Parents can customize the interfaces, but you're generally going to have apps, games, ebooks, and videos to work with. Amazon Kids includes two interfaces, one for very young kids and one for kids around 6-14. The latter is similar to a regular adult Fire Tablet UI with more restrictions, while the former is extremely simplistic with big icons and very few options. Kids can choose their own profile icons and wallpaper. Google Kids Space is sort of in the middle of Amazon's two age groups. The Play Store has a larger library of apps, but Amazon is king when it comes to ebooks. Truthfully, content isn't really the defining feature of either of these services. You will most likely be able to find anything you want on both of them. The key is parental control, so let's talk about that. As you would expect, both Amazon Kids and Google Kids Space offer a wide variety of parental controls. However, they're vastly different. For example, in Amazon Kids, the only thing that can be accessed outside of the home screen is a handful of Android Quick Settings. However, the worst thing about Google Kids Space is how easy it is for a child to access parental controls. All they have to do is long-press the button in the bottom corner—there's no PIN or any security. Amazon is constantly asking for a PIN (as it should). As briefly mentioned, Amazon Kids and Google Kids Space both have optional subscription services to enhance the experience. Amazon Kids+ is $4.99 per month. It includes additional ebooks, movies, TV shows, games, apps, and Alexa Skills. The content has been curated, and it includes brands such as PBS Kids, Disney, Nickelodeon, LEGO, Sesame Street, and Marvel. Google Kids Space works with Google Play Pass , which is essentially a "Netflix but for Google Play" type service. For kids, it unlocks additional premium content from Google Play that doesn't have ads or in-app purchases. Play Pass is also $4.99 per month. The story on device compatibility is pretty straightforward. Amazon Kids is available on Amazon Fire tablets, and you don't actually need a special Kids model to use it. Google Kids Space is available on select Android tablets from Lenovo, onn, Google, Nokia, Medion, and Multilaser. You can also attempt to install the app yourself . So, the natural question is, which one should you choose for your child? Both Amazon and Google have pretty nice offerings, but there are certain advantages of each one. Amazon Kids is better for kids under 5 years old. The UI is simpler and extremely locked down. I have no worries at all about my son getting into something he shouldn't. In fact, that's another area where Amazon wins: control. You can restrict Amazon Kids much more than you can Google Kids Space. For example, let's say you really just had one app you wanted your kid to be able to use. That's it. You will have an easier time doing that with Amazon Kids than you would with Google Kids Space. However, the fact that the controls are only available remotely via a browser is annoying. I'd love a Parent Dashboard app. Google Kids Space is better for kids who are a bit older and have a bit more freedom. The avatar customizer is super fun, and the UI generally looks a lot more modern and clean. You can't turn off as much stuff on Kids Space as you can on Amazon Kids, but you can limit what kind of content is recommended. If I had to pick an overall winner, it would be Amazon Kids. Amazon has been doing this longer, the parental controls are more granular, and Fire tablets are easier to find. However, Google Kids Space is a worthy competitor for older kids. passages: Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday.
In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.
“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.
She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft.
When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.
Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”
MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom
The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended.

sources.title: Margaret Hamilton, pioneering Apollo program software engineer, dies at 90
passages: Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.

By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

She said "coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure," and that because software was "a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust." Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. “Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great grandchildren, according to MIT. Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman paid tribute on X, calling Hamilton "a pioneer whose work helped make Apollo and humanity's first journeys to the moon possible." The Apollo program allowed the United States to beat the Soviet Union in the race to land the first humans on the Moon.

Hamilton was born in Indiana in 1936 and studied mathematics before moving to Boston, Massachusetts, with her husband in 1959. She found work at MIT in meteorology before joining a lab in 1965 that was seeking people to develop software to "send a man to the Moon." MIT said she "was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project." "By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of (Apollo's) Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo's software," the university said.

Former President Barack Obama awarded Hamilton the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. In 2009, she told MIT News: "There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s." She said "coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure," and that because software was "a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust." "Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers," she said.
Hamilton went on to publish more than 130 papers and started her own software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies. — AFP

extraction.body: My Decoder guest today is Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, and we’re discussing the new wave of consumer-friendly AI agents. If you’ve been paying attention to this space, you know AI enthusiasts have been using agents for a minute now — homebrew OpenClaw setups led to a surge in Mac Mini sales earlier this year. But the launches of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and xAI’s Grok Bot have brought easy-to-use agents to millions. Muse and Dots have had the highest-profile product launches, and they’re fascinating to pit against each other. In OpenAI’s cases, the company is even offering “specialist” Dots for marketing, legal work, and accounting. So you’ll hear Hayden and me get into why Meta, which still doesn’t have a frontier model of its own, might have a meaningful edge here because it’s so much better at making and distributing consumer products. There’s also a huge Decoder-style tension wrapped up in the agent race: a conversation about what AI is good at today, what it still can’t do, and then the privacy and security implications of handing over your credit card information, your email inbox, and other sensitive hard drive data to an AI that might be able to do things for you without even requiring an app or a phone in your hand. That might be the future of all computing, but it’s not at all clear if most people want to hand over the data to make it happen. Okay: The Verge’s Hayden Field on Muse, Dots, and trusting AI agents. Alexandr Wang from Meta has maybe been taking some shots, but none of the Real Housewives stuff we usually end up talking about when you’re on the show. Yeah, just some good old-fashioned product competition in the marketplace. Hayden, you were at OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco. The company announced Dots, which is their new agent platform with a cute mascot. That happened just a few weeks after Meta Connect, at which the company was all in on Muse, their agent platform with an adorable mascot. It’s funny to me because I’ve been covering agents for so long. I remember that in 2022, it was the year of ideation — that’s what tech leaders called it, referring to agents. They didn’t have any names for those years, but agents were still pretty bad, as we saw. 2026 seems, to me, like the year of the beginnings of actually useful AI agents for the consumer, like always-on autonomous agents. Obviously, OpenAI was the start of all of this. But what’s interesting to me is that one man, Peter Steinberger, was able to create an actually useful AI agent for the consumer with OpenClaw — an always-on tool, despite its privacy flaws. But it was an agent that was useful enough that people still wanted to use it anyway and try to find ways around these privacy issues that it was having. That inspired these companies to say, “If one man can do this over the course of one weekend, we’ve really been slacking. We have to get it together.” OpenAI hired that guy, and now we have Dots. Meta, of course, was working on its own version of this and put it out sooner with Muse. They’re basically both always-on, autonomous AI agents that these companies are peddling as a way to be your personal assistant in a lot of ways. The idea is to use them for booking flights, booking dinner reservations, buying gifts for people, but not only that. Some of them, Dots in particular, are kind of going further to be your work personal assistant and we’ll get into that in a minute. But this is where OpenAI and Meta are warring right now. They’re trying to present these two AI agents as a little bit different from each other, even though they’re essentially the same. Just broadly speaking, to define some terms, we’re gonna keep saying “agent,” and what we mean here is an AI model wrapped in a harness that lets it use a computer. The way that I describe AI agents usually is an AI tool that can complete multi-step complex tasks on your behalf without you hand-holding it the whole time. I was a personal assistant in one of my first jobs in New York, so I would’ve gotten fired if every time my boss asked me to book a flight for her, I said, “What time? Also, what’s your loyalty number again, for this other thing? This is what they’re pitching these AI agents as — things that can work on their own mental kind of scratchpad in the background and not ask you every single time there’s a step. Just to say it clearly, both Muse and Dots come out of the OpenClaw lineage, which is a technical approach to building an agent, right? There are a lot of different ways you might be able to accomplish “It’ll remember your SkyMiles number and book you a flight.” But the way everyone’s going at it now is the idea of a harness around a model.

sources.title: OpenAI Dots vs Meta Muse vs Grok Bot: How the Three Always-On AI Agents Compare
passages: OpenAI Dots: the knowledge-work agent OpenAI describes Dots as “remarkably capable, always-on agents built to handle everything.” The practical product, at launch, is narrower and more useful than that line.
Between 11 August and 29 September 2026, SpaceXAI, Meta, and OpenAI each released an always-on agent that keeps working after the chat window closes.
Grok Bot had a 49-day head start on Dots and a 28-day head start on Muse.
OpenAI Dots closed the sequence at DevDay on 29 September.
Grok Bot sits inside a roster of role-based teammates.
All three give the agent its own computer in the cloud, a browser, permission to use connected apps, and a rule that sensitive steps come back for approval.

Inside OpenAI, the company described dots investigating a bug the moment it is mentioned in Slack, turning a finished design into a working app, and preparing an invoice an early tester had forgotten to send — after approval.
Muse sits inside personal life and messaging.

extraction.body: Between 11 August and 29 September 2026, SpaceXAI, Meta, and OpenAI each released an always-on agent that keeps working after the chat window closes. OpenAI Dots closed the sequence at DevDay on 29 September. All three give the agent its own computer in the cloud, a browser, permission to use connected apps, and a rule that sensitive steps come back for approval. Each product is aimed at a different job, a different set of apps, and a different buyer. Treating them as three versions of one assistant is the fastest way to pick the wrong one. What “always-on” actually means A chatbot waits for a prompt and ends when the session ends. An always-on agent is given a goal, a boundary, and a machine, then continues between conversations. Three design choices show up in all three products: A dedicated cloud computer. The agent is not borrowing the user’s laptop by default. Work can continue after the laptop is closed. The user can open that computer and inspect what is happening. The agent can browse, fill forms, draft messages, update records, and prepare files. Each product says it learns preferences, standards, and unfinished work, then uses that context the next time. The split is in whose day the agent is meant to run. Muse sits inside personal life and messaging. Grok Bot sits inside a roster of role-based teammates. The six-week timeline DateProductWhat shipped11 August 2026Grok BotBeta launch. Always-on teammates on a shared cloud computer, for higher-tier SuperGrok and Cursor plans at first.21–26 August 2026Grok BotAccess widened. By 26 August it was included on SuperGrok plans and paid Cursor plans, including Cursor Pro.29 August 2026Grok BotX connector, with X API credits for paid users.8 September 2026Meta MuseConsumer launch in the United States, on iOS, Android, and the web, with WhatsApp as a channel.23–24 September 2026Meta MuseConnect 2026 additions: deeper app integrations, glasses plans, and a stated path to a Muse email address.29 September 2026OpenAI DotsDevDay launch. Grok Bot had a 49-day head start on Dots and a 28-day head start on Muse. That lead is about product shape, not about a finished category. All three were still in early rollout in the first days of October 2026. OpenAI Dots: the knowledge-work agent OpenAI describes Dots as “remarkably capable, always-on agents built to handle everything.” The practical product, at launch, is narrower and more useful than that line. A dot is a named agent inside ChatGPT, powered by GPT-6 Astra, with its own cloud computer and browser, able to connect to more than 4,000 apps through ChatGPT plugins. Context is meant to carry across those channels, so a project started in ChatGPT can be followed in Slack without a fresh briefing. A dot is a standing assignment, not a single chat. OpenAI’s examples are all professional: A developer’s dot watches customer feedback, scopes small fixes, builds and tests them, and returns pull requests with videos of the change. A launch lead’s dot revises positioning and draft assets when product scope changes. A sales lead’s dot checks requirements against product docs, builds a proof of concept, and updates the proposal. Inside OpenAI, the company described dots investigating a bug the moment it is mentioned in Slack, turning a finished design into a working app, and preparing an invoice an early tester had forgotten to send — after approval. Controls, and what a dot will not do on its own The user’s own computer stays isolated unless it is deliberately connected, and that connection starts off. For supported sites, a dot can use saved passwords without exposing them to the model. When the user is not actively directing it, “proactive research” runs through read-only tools. In that mode it cannot send messages, change app content, or control the browser or computer. Dots start with built-in rules for when to act and when to ask. Auto-review checks steps that could affect accounts or share information.

With coverage on everything from exciting product launches to essential software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . If you blinked this month, you might think Meta and OpenAI launched essentially the same AI agent three weeks apart. On September 8, Meta launched Muse , a personal AI agent that gets its own dedicated cloud computer and keeps working on your tasks after you close the app. Twenty-one days later, OpenAI took the stage at DevDay 2026 in San Francisco and unveiled Dots — always-on AI agents inside ChatGPT, each running on its own cloud computer and browser. And while they sound remarkably similar, with reports across the internet comparing them because of a few similarities like the fact that both get their own cloud computer, work after you leave, and can connect to outside services, that's about where the comparisons stop. Muse and Dots are not interchangeable. These are different companies, different models and very different products. Most importantly for your wallet, they're aimed at different customers. Muse is free to start and was built for everyday people and small businesses. Dots starts with a $100-a-month Pro plan and is clearly aimed at professionals and developer teams. Here's what you actually need to know about each one, where they overlap and which one matters to you right now. Meta Muse: A personal agent powered by Muse Spark and runs inside its own Muse Secure VM, giving it a dedicated cloud computer and browser where it can continue working after you leave. Muse is available in the U.S. and Canada with a free tier, alongside $20 and $100 monthly plans. You can use it on iOS, Android and the web, while Meta has expanded Muse with Mac app control, its own email address, AI glasses support and the Muse Charm companion device. Its Sentinel permissions system separates read and write access, and Muse can connect to services including Asana, Slack, Shopify, Stripe, Zoom, QuickBooks and Notion, as well as Facebook and Instagram business accounts. ChatGPT Dots: Each dot is powered by GPT-6 Astra and gets its own dedicated cloud computer and browser, allowing it to continue working in the background after you leave ChatGPT. Dots are available to eligible ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium subscribers, with Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare access through an admin-enabled beta. You can interact with a dot through ChatGPT on the web, desktop and mobile, as well as Slack and Microsoft Teams, with voice calling available and texting in beta. Dots can connect to more than 4,000 apps through ChatGPT's plugin ecosystem and use custom rules, approval requirements and auto-review to govern what they're allowed to do. For now, users get one primary dot, although OpenAI has previewed specialist dots and a future where multiple dots can work together. Both tools update you asynchronously and come back for approval before doing anything consequential. The idea that an autonomous agent shouldn't be able to send, spend or make sensitive changes without you is quickly becoming table stakes for this category. Muse is Meta's version for a personal AI agent, and the company made one huge bet that OpenAI hasn't: making it free to start. The product is goal-first rather than chat-first. You give Muse something to accomplish — running parts of your business, finding new customers or handling logistics, for example — and it builds a plan, continues working after you close the app and returns when something changes or requires your approval. Muse runs inside what Meta calls the Muse Secure VM, a dedicated cloud environment with its own browser that holds the agent and your data. You can set its name, avatar and communication style, watch its browser work and govern what it can touch through Sentinel, Meta's permissions system separating read access from write access. Meta has gradually been expanding where Muse can operate. It now includes macOS app control, an email address of the agent's own and support for interacting with it through Meta's smart glasses. Meta has also announced integrations and commerce partnerships spanning services including Stripe, Shopify, Walmart , Expedia and Instacart. Muse for Small Business pushes that further with third-party app connectors including Asana, Box, Canva, Dropbox, Figma, QuickBooks, Notion, Shopify, Slack, Stripe and Zoom, alongside access to Facebook and Instagram business accounts. These aren't a separate agent but additional capabilities inside Muse. Dots take the same basic always-on agent architecture in a very different direction. CEO Sam Altman described them as "remarkably capable, always-on agents" during OpenAI's DevDay presentation and said the company's ambitions for Dots extend beyond ChatGPT itself. Each dot runs on GPT-6 Astra, gets its own cloud computer and browser and can connect to more than 4,000 apps through ChatGPT's plugin ecosystem. You give it a goal — monitoring a pipeline, managing a recurring workflow or researching something over several days — and the dot can continue pursuing it around the clock, sending updates and asking for your input when it reaches a boundary. Dots can learn preferences over time and use read-only tools for some proactive background research. OpenAI also keeps particularly sensitive actions, including changing passwords, in human hands. At launch, each person gets one primary dot they can name and customize with an avatar. OpenAI has also previewed "specialist dots" for companies and is working with Microsoft to bring the agents under Agent 365's management and security controls. The longer-term vision is effectively a team of specialized agents working alongside people. Once set up, a dot can be reached through ChatGPT on mobile and web as well as services including Slack and Microsoft Teams. ChatGPT Space provides a shared environment where teammates and dots can work together on projects. But there's a major catch: most ChatGPT users can't try one. Dots are rolling out to ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium subscribers, while Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare workspaces get an admin-enabled beta. Free and Plus subscribers are locked out for now. Pro 100, at $100 per month, is the entry point. OpenAI also offers Pro 200 and Pro 500 tiers, while Business Premium costs $125 per user each month. Pro subscribers in the EEA, Switzerland and UK also can't use Dots yet. Put the technical similarities aside and the biggest distinction becomes obvious. Muse starts at $0. Dots start at $100 a month. This alone tells you who Meta and OpenAI expect to use these products. Meta is trying to put an autonomous agent in the hands of ordinary consumers and small businesses. OpenAI is starting with professionals, teams and organizations already willing to spend significantly more on AI. That difference runs through almost every other decision the companies have made. Muse is a standalone product built around the agent itself. It has a personality you shape, a Feed and Goals you can check, mobile apps, the palm-sized Muse Charm and integration with Meta's glasses. It feels like Meta is asking what happens when an AI agent becomes another personal device or service in your life. OpenAI built Dots into ChatGPT. The agent is another capability of a platform professionals and businesses may already use, and OpenAI is putting it in places where work already happens, including Slack and Teams. ChatGPT Space and the planned specialist dots push the concept even further toward people and agents sharing the same workplace. The underlying idea may be similar. The products built around it aren't. It's free to start, built around individual users and now has enough small-business integrations to make it useful beyond simple personal tasks. The trade-off is that giving an autonomous agent access to accounts, communications and other services requires paying close attention to its permissions, particularly given the early scrutiny around Muse. If you're already paying for ChatGPT Pro or you're choosing an agent for a business, you've probably already found a use for Dots. OpenAI has made its professional and enterprise ambitions pretty clear. For everyone else, there's little reason to pay $100 a month just to get Dots right now, particularly when OpenAI hasn't made them available to Plus subscribers. Muse wants to become your personal AI helper. Dots wants to become an always-on member of your team. They may have arrived three weeks apart with remarkably similar technology underneath, but they're not really fighting for the same user — at least not yet. extraction.body: My Decoder guest today is Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, and we’re discussing the new wave of consumer-friendly AI agents. If you’ve been paying attention to this space, you know AI enthusiasts have been using agents for a minute now — homebrew OpenClaw setups led to a surge in Mac Mini sales earlier this year. But the launches of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and xAI’s Grok Bot have brought easy-to-use agents to millions. Muse and Dots have had the highest-profile product launches, and they’re fascinating to pit against each other. In OpenAI’s cases, the company is even offering “specialist” Dots for marketing, legal work, and accounting. So you’ll hear Hayden and me get into why Meta, which still doesn’t have a frontier model of its own, might have a meaningful edge here because it’s so much better at making and distributing consumer products. There’s also a huge Decoder-style tension wrapped up in the agent race: a conversation about what AI is good at today, what it still can’t do, and then the privacy and security implications of handing over your credit card information, your email inbox, and other sensitive hard drive data to an AI that might be able to do things for you without even requiring an app or a phone in your hand. That might be the future of all computing, but it’s not at all clear if most people want to hand over the data to make it happen. Okay: The Verge’s Hayden Field on Muse, Dots, and trusting AI agents. Alexandr Wang from Meta has maybe been taking some shots, but none of the Real Housewives stuff we usually end up talking about when you’re on the show. Yeah, just some good old-fashioned product competition in the marketplace. Hayden, you were at OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco. The company announced Dots, which is their new agent platform with a cute mascot. That happened just a few weeks after Meta Connect, at which the company was all in on Muse, their agent platform with an adorable mascot. It’s funny to me because I’ve been covering agents for so long. I remember that in 2022, it was the year of ideation — that’s what tech leaders called it, referring to agents. They didn’t have any names for those years, but agents were still pretty bad, as we saw. 2026 seems, to me, like the year of the beginnings of actually useful AI agents for the consumer, like always-on autonomous agents. Obviously, OpenAI was the start of all of this. But what’s interesting to me is that one man, Peter Steinberger, was able to create an actually useful AI agent for the consumer with OpenClaw — an always-on tool, despite its privacy flaws. But it was an agent that was useful enough that people still wanted to use it anyway and try to find ways around these privacy issues that it was having. That inspired these companies to say, “If one man can do this over the course of one weekend, we’ve really been slacking. We have to get it together.” OpenAI hired that guy, and now we have Dots. Meta, of course, was working on its own version of this and put it out sooner with Muse. They’re basically both always-on, autonomous AI agents that these companies are peddling as a way to be your personal assistant in a lot of ways. The idea is to use them for booking flights, booking dinner reservations, buying gifts for people, but not only that. Some of them, Dots in particular, are kind of going further to be your work personal assistant and we’ll get into that in a minute. But this is where OpenAI and Meta are warring right now. They’re trying to present these two AI agents as a little bit different from each other, even though they’re essentially the same. Just broadly speaking, to define some terms, we’re gonna keep saying “agent,” and what we mean here is an AI model wrapped in a harness that lets it use a computer. The way that I describe AI agents usually is an AI tool that can complete multi-step complex tasks on your behalf without you hand-holding it the whole time. I was a personal assistant in one of my first jobs in New York, so I would’ve gotten fired if every time my boss asked me to book a flight for her, I said, “What time? Also, what’s your loyalty number again, for this other thing? This is what they’re pitching these AI agents as — things that can work on their own mental kind of scratchpad in the background and not ask you every single time there’s a step. Just to say it clearly, both Muse and Dots come out of the OpenClaw lineage, which is a technical approach to building an agent, right? There are a lot of different ways you might be able to accomplish “It’ll remember your SkyMiles number and book you a flight.” But the way everyone’s going at it now is the idea of a harness around a model.

extraction.body: Between 11 August and 29 September 2026, SpaceXAI, Meta, and OpenAI each released an always-on agent that keeps working after the chat window closes. OpenAI Dots closed the sequence at DevDay on 29 September. All three give the agent its own computer in the cloud, a browser, permission to use connected apps, and a rule that sensitive steps come back for approval. Each product is aimed at a different job, a different set of apps, and a different buyer. Treating them as three versions of one assistant is the fastest way to pick the wrong one. What “always-on” actually means A chatbot waits for a prompt and ends when the session ends. An always-on agent is given a goal, a boundary, and a machine, then continues between conversations. Three design choices show up in all three products: A dedicated cloud computer. The agent is not borrowing the user’s laptop by default. Work can continue after the laptop is closed. The user can open that computer and inspect what is happening. The agent can browse, fill forms, draft messages, update records, and prepare files. Muse is available in the U.S. and Canada with a free tier, alongside $20 and $100 monthly plans.

Meta has gradually been expanding where Muse can operate.
Muse is a standalone product built around the agent itself.
It feels like Meta is asking what happens when an AI agent becomes another personal device or service in your life.
ChatGPT Space and the planned specialist dots push the concept even further toward people and agents sharing the same workplace.
If you're already paying for ChatGPT Pro or you're choosing an agent for a business, you've probably already found a use for Dots.
These aren't a separate agent but additional capabilities inside Muse.
Dots take the same basic always-on agent architecture in a very different direction.
Meta is trying to put an autonomous agent in the hands of ordinary consumers and small businesses.
For everyone else, there's little reason to pay $100 a month just to get Dots right now, particularly when OpenAI hasn't made them available to Plus subscribers.

With coverage on everything from exciting product launches to essential software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . If you blinked this month, you might think Meta and OpenAI launched essentially the same AI agent three weeks apart. On September 8, Meta launched Muse , a personal AI agent that gets its own dedicated cloud computer and keeps working on your tasks after you close the app. Twenty-one days later, OpenAI took the stage at DevDay 2026 in San Francisco and unveiled Dots — always-on AI agents inside ChatGPT, each running on its own cloud computer and browser. And while they sound remarkably similar, with reports across the internet comparing them because of a few similarities like the fact that both get their own cloud computer, work after you leave, and can connect to outside services, that's about where the comparisons stop. Muse and Dots are not interchangeable. These are different companies, different models and very different products. Most importantly for your wallet, they're aimed at different customers. Muse is free to start and was built for everyday people and small businesses. Dots starts with a $100-a-month Pro plan and is clearly aimed at professionals and developer teams. Here's what you actually need to know about each one, where they overlap and which one matters to you right now. Meta Muse: A personal agent powered by Muse Spark and runs inside its own Muse Secure VM, giving it a dedicated cloud computer and browser where it can continue working after you leave. Muse is available in the U.S. and Canada with a free tier, alongside $20 and $100 monthly plans. You can use it on iOS, Android and the web, while Meta has expanded Muse with Mac app control, its own email address, AI glasses support and the Muse Charm companion device. Its Sentinel permissions system separates read and write access, and Muse can connect to services including Asana, Slack, Shopify, Stripe, Zoom, QuickBooks and Notion, as well as Facebook and Instagram business accounts. ChatGPT Dots: Each dot is powered by GPT-6 Astra and gets its own dedicated cloud computer and browser, allowing it to continue working in the background after you leave ChatGPT. Dots are available to eligible ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium subscribers, with Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare access through an admin-enabled beta. You can interact with a dot through ChatGPT on the web, desktop and mobile, as well as Slack and Microsoft Teams, with voice calling available and texting in beta. Dots can connect to more than 4,000 apps through ChatGPT's plugin ecosystem and use custom rules, approval requirements and auto-review to govern what they're allowed to do. For now, users get one primary dot, although OpenAI has previewed specialist dots and a future where multiple dots can work together. Both tools update you asynchronously and come back for approval before doing anything consequential. The idea that an autonomous agent shouldn't be able to send, spend or make sensitive changes without you is quickly becoming table stakes for this category. Muse is Meta's version for a personal AI agent, and the company made one huge bet that OpenAI hasn't: making it free to start. The product is goal-first rather than chat-first. You give Muse something to accomplish — running parts of your business, finding new customers or handling logistics, for example — and it builds a plan, continues working after you close the app and returns when something changes or requires your approval. Muse runs inside what Meta calls the Muse Secure VM, a dedicated cloud environment with its own browser that holds the agent and your data. You can set its name, avatar and communication style, watch its browser work and govern what it can touch through Sentinel, Meta's permissions system separating read access from write access. Meta has gradually been expanding where Muse can operate. It now includes macOS app control, an email address of the agent's own and support for interacting with it through Meta's smart glasses. Meta has also announced integrations and commerce partnerships spanning services including Stripe, Shopify, Walmart , Expedia and Instacart. Muse for Small Business pushes that further with third-party app connectors including Asana, Box, Canva, Dropbox, Figma, QuickBooks, Notion, Shopify, Slack, Stripe and Zoom, alongside access to Facebook and Instagram business accounts. These aren't a separate agent but additional capabilities inside Muse. Dots take the same basic always-on agent architecture in a very different direction. CEO Sam Altman described them as "remarkably capable, always-on agents" during OpenAI's DevDay presentation and said the company's ambitions for Dots extend beyond ChatGPT itself. Each dot runs on GPT-6 Astra, gets its own cloud computer and browser and can connect to more than 4,000 apps through ChatGPT's plugin ecosystem. You give it a goal — monitoring a pipeline, managing a recurring workflow or researching something over several days — and the dot can continue pursuing it around the clock, sending updates and asking for your input when it reaches a boundary. Dots can learn preferences over time and use read-only tools for some proactive background research. OpenAI also keeps particularly sensitive actions, including changing passwords, in human hands. At launch, each person gets one primary dot they can name and customize with an avatar. OpenAI has also previewed "specialist dots" for companies and is working with Microsoft to bring the agents under Agent 365's management and security controls. The longer-term vision is effectively a team of specialized agents working alongside people. Once set up, a dot can be reached through ChatGPT on mobile and web as well as services including Slack and Microsoft Teams. ChatGPT Space provides a shared environment where teammates and dots can work together on projects. But there's a major catch: most ChatGPT users can't try one. Dots are rolling out to ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium subscribers, while Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare workspaces get an admin-enabled beta. Free and Plus subscribers are locked out for now. Pro 100, at $100 per month, is the entry point. OpenAI also offers Pro 200 and Pro 500 tiers, while Business Premium costs $125 per user each month. Pro subscribers in the EEA, Switzerland and UK also can't use Dots yet. Put the technical similarities aside and the biggest distinction becomes obvious. Muse starts at $0. Dots start at $100 a month. This alone tells you who Meta and OpenAI expect to use these products. Meta is trying to put an autonomous agent in the hands of ordinary consumers and small businesses. OpenAI is starting with professionals, teams and organizations already willing to spend significantly more on AI. That difference runs through almost every other decision the companies have made. Muse is a standalone product built around the agent itself. It has a personality you shape, a Feed and Goals you can check, mobile apps, the palm-sized Muse Charm and integration with Meta's glasses. It feels like Meta is asking what happens when an AI agent becomes another personal device or service in your life. OpenAI built Dots into ChatGPT. The agent is another capability of a platform professionals and businesses may already use, and OpenAI is putting it in places where work already happens, including Slack and Teams. ChatGPT Space and the planned specialist dots push the concept even further toward people and agents sharing the same workplace. The underlying idea may be similar. The products built around it aren't. It's free to start, built around individual users and now has enough small-business integrations to make it useful beyond simple personal tasks. The trade-off is that giving an autonomous agent access to accounts, communications and other services requires paying close attention to its permissions, particularly given the early scrutiny around Muse. If you're already paying for ChatGPT Pro or you're choosing an agent for a business, you've probably already found a use for Dots. OpenAI has made its professional and enterprise ambitions pretty clear. For everyone else, there's little reason to pay $100 a month just to get Dots right now, particularly when OpenAI hasn't made them available to Plus subscribers. Muse wants to become your personal AI helper. Dots wants to become an always-on member of your team. They may have arrived three weeks apart with remarkably similar technology underneath, but they're not really fighting for the same user — at least not yet. extraction.body: Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90. Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering". Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September. "To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division. It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon. "I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring. The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved. But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT. The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her. Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969 In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel. At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space". Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958. She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree. From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts. "We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media. "Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Hamilton being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then President Barack Obama in 2016

I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency. Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended. “It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said. Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. “Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great grandchildren, according to MIT. Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

Her team’s error-recovery design helped keep Apollo 11’s landing on track.
More than 400 people worked on Apollo software across the wider programme, MIT says: her leadership was significant, but the code was a collective effort.

The familiar photograph of Hamilton beside an Apollo code printout captures the work’s scale, but not the team behind it.
Hamilton’s principles remain relevant as software affects transport, medicine, finance, public services and artificial-intelligence tools.
Hamilton’s work helped establish that software should be judged by how it behaves under pressure, not only by what it can do in a demonstration.
NASA’s transcript shows a chain of software behaviour, engineering knowledge and human judgment—not a solitary act by Hamilton.

Margaret Hamilton, who led Apollo flight-software work at MIT, has died at 90. Her team’s error-recovery design helped keep Apollo 11’s landing on track. Correction (October 8, 2026): An earlier headline said Hamilton “coined” software engineering. MIT describes her using the term, but does not establish she originated it. The headline and article have been revised. Margaret Hamilton, who led Apollo flight-software teams at MIT, died on September 30 at 90, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology announced. Her work helped make software reliability a central engineering problem when code was still often treated as an uncertain add-on to hardware. Hamilton is remembered for alarms during Apollo 11’s lunar descent, but the fuller story is not that one programmer “saved” the landing. A large team designed a computer system to recover from overload, while astronauts and mission controllers interpreted its warnings and chose how to proceed. Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a mathematics degree and a minor in philosophy. She began programming at MIT in 1959, working on weather software with meteorologist Edward Lorenz. In 1961 she joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory’s SAGE air-defence project, writing software for a system that helped the US Air Force detect potentially hostile aircraft. MIT says that work sharpened her interest in reliability, then a relatively new concern in software. Hamilton joined MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory in 1965 after it won NASA’s contract for Apollo flight software. She began on uncrewed missions and later led teams developing software for crewed flights. By 1968 she was an assistant director overseeing the Command and Service Module team. More than 400 people worked on Apollo software across the wider programme, MIT says: her leadership was significant, but the code was a collective effort. The Apollo Guidance Computer had to manage navigation and control with severe limits on memory and processing time. Software helped execute flight plans and keep essential guidance tasks running when demands competed. Hamilton and colleagues worked on error handling, testing and priority scheduling—the rules that determine which work matters most when a computer is overloaded. During Apollo 11’s descent on July 20, 1969, the lunar module computer displayed a 1202 program alarm, followed by a 1201 alarm. NASA’s Apollo 11 historical record traces the overload to unexpected rendezvous-radar data. The computer had more requests than its limited resources could handle; the alarm told the crew and controllers it had reached a limit. The recovery mechanism restarted the computer and resumed selected tasks, preserving critical guidance and display functions rather than every lower-priority job. The alarms did not by themselves prove the flight was safe. Guidance expert Steve Bales assessed the situation in Houston, and CAPCOM Charlie Duke relayed the “go” call; the astronauts managed the approach. NASA’s transcript shows a chain of software behaviour, engineering knowledge and human judgment—not a solitary act by Hamilton. The system did not erase the source of the overload or make every possible failure harmless. It made the condition visible, responded according to priority and gave trained people information to decide whether to continue. Hamilton argued that software deserved the seriousness given to other engineering disciplines and should be treated as part of systems engineering. She later founded software companies focused on error prevention and reliability. Her career helped give software engineering professional weight at a time when the field was still taking shape. She was also the first programmer hired for MIT’s Apollo project and its first woman programmer, according to MIT. NASA recognised her contributions with the Exceptional Space Act Award in 2003; President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. The familiar photograph of Hamilton beside an Apollo code printout captures the work’s scale, but not the team behind it. Hamilton’s principles remain relevant as software affects transport, medicine, finance, public services and artificial-intelligence tools. Modern generative AI is not Apollo flight software: it can produce uncertain, plausible-sounding answers, while Apollo’s code was engineered for defined functions. NIST lists confabulation—confidently presented false output—among generative AI risks. The connection is not equivalence but the need for testing, clear limits and a plan for failure. For AI agents that use digital tools, a polished response is not enough. Developers must consider what a system is allowed to do, how it signals uncertainty, what happens when a tool fails and when a person must approve an action. Safety is designed across software, hardware, procedures, operators and rules—not delivered by a single celebrated feature. Hamilton’s work helped establish that software should be judged by how it behaves under pressure, not only by what it can do in a demonstration. Apollo’s engineering lesson was to build, test and improve a system for the unexpected. MIT says Hamilton is survived by her daughter, son-in-law, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and siblings. A memorial service is planned for spring in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Her legacy endures in a question every high-stakes digital system must answer: when something goes wrong, what has the design prepared it to do next? No sign-in required. Choose up to two. extraction.body: Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90. Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering". Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September. "To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream. Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division. It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon. "I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring. The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved. But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT. The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her. Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969 In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel. At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space". Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958. She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree. From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts. "We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media. "Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Hamilton being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then President Barack Obama in 2016

Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

Margaret Hamilton, who led Apollo flight-software work at MIT, has died at 90. Her team’s error-recovery design helped keep Apollo 11’s landing on track. Correction (October 8, 2026): An earlier headline said Hamilton “coined” software engineering. MIT describes her using the term, but does not establish she originated it. The headline and article have been revised. Margaret Hamilton, who led Apollo flight-software teams at MIT, died on September 30 at 90, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology announced. Her work helped make software reliability a central engineering problem when code was still often treated as an uncertain add-on to hardware. Hamilton is remembered for alarms during Apollo 11’s lunar descent, but the fuller story is not that one programmer “saved” the landing. A large team designed a computer system to recover from overload, while astronauts and mission controllers interpreted its warnings and chose how to proceed. Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a mathematics degree and a minor in philosophy. She began programming at MIT in 1959, working on weather software with meteorologist Edward Lorenz. In 1961 she joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory’s SAGE air-defence project, writing software for a system that helped the US Air Force detect potentially hostile aircraft. MIT says that work sharpened her interest in reliability, then a relatively new concern in software. Hamilton joined MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory in 1965 after it won NASA’s contract for Apollo flight software. She began on uncrewed missions and later led teams developing software for crewed flights. By 1968 she was an assistant director overseeing the Command and Service Module team. More than 400 people worked on Apollo software across the wider programme, MIT says: her leadership was significant, but the code was a collective effort. The Apollo Guidance Computer had to manage navigation and control with severe limits on memory and processing time. Software helped execute flight plans and keep essential guidance tasks running when demands competed. Hamilton and colleagues worked on error handling, testing and priority scheduling—the rules that determine which work matters most when a computer is overloaded. During Apollo 11’s descent on July 20, 1969, the lunar module computer displayed a 1202 program alarm, followed by a 1201 alarm. NASA’s Apollo 11 historical record traces the overload to unexpected rendezvous-radar data. The computer had more requests than its limited resources could handle; the alarm told the crew and controllers it had reached a limit. The recovery mechanism restarted the computer and resumed selected tasks, preserving critical guidance and display functions rather than every lower-priority job. The alarms did not by themselves prove the flight was safe. Guidance expert Steve Bales assessed the situation in Houston, and CAPCOM Charlie Duke relayed the “go” call; the astronauts managed the approach. NASA’s transcript shows a chain of software behaviour, engineering knowledge and human judgment—not a solitary act by Hamilton. The system did not erase the source of the overload or make every possible failure harmless. It made the condition visible, responded according to priority and gave trained people information to decide whether to continue. Hamilton argued that software deserved the seriousness given to other engineering disciplines and should be treated as part of systems engineering. She later founded software companies focused on error prevention and reliability. Her career helped give software engineering professional weight at a time when the field was still taking shape. She was also the first programmer hired for MIT’s Apollo project and its first woman programmer, according to MIT. NASA recognised her contributions with the Exceptional Space Act Award in 2003; President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. The familiar photograph of Hamilton beside an Apollo code printout captures the work’s scale, but not the team behind it. Hamilton’s principles remain relevant as software affects transport, medicine, finance, public services and artificial-intelligence tools. Modern generative AI is not Apollo flight software: it can produce uncertain, plausible-sounding answers, while Apollo’s code was engineered for defined functions. NIST lists confabulation—confidently presented false output—among generative AI risks. The connection is not equivalence but the need for testing, clear limits and a plan for failure. For AI agents that use digital tools, a polished response is not enough. Developers must consider what a system is allowed to do, how it signals uncertainty, what happens when a tool fails and when a person must approve an action. Safety is designed across software, hardware, procedures, operators and rules—not delivered by a single celebrated feature. Hamilton’s work helped establish that software should be judged by how it behaves under pressure, not only by what it can do in a demonstration. Apollo’s engineering lesson was to build, test and improve a system for the unexpected. MIT says Hamilton is survived by her daughter, son-in-law, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and siblings. A memorial service is planned for spring in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Her legacy endures in a question every high-stakes digital system must answer: when something goes wrong, what has the design prepared it to do next? No sign-in required. Choose up to two. Software helped execute flight plans and keep essential guidance tasks running when demands competed. Hamilton and colleagues worked on error handling, testing and priority scheduling—the rules that determine which work matters most when a computer is overloaded.

During Apollo 11’s descent on July 20, 1969, the lunar module computer displayed a 1202 program alarm, followed by a 1201 alarm. NASA’s Apollo 11 historical record traces the overload to unexpected rendezvous-radar data. The computer had more requests than its limited resources could handle; the alarm told the crew and controllers it had reached a limit.

The recovery mechanism restarted the computer and resumed selected tasks, preserving critical guidance and display functions rather than every lower-priority job. The alarms did not by themselves prove the flight was safe. Guidance expert Steve Bales assessed the situation in Houston, and CAPCOM Charlie Duke relayed the “go” call; the astronauts managed the approach. NASA’s transcript shows a chain of software behaviour, engineering knowledge and human judgment—not a solitary act by Hamilton.

The system did not erase the source of the overload or make every possible failure harmless. It made the condition visible, responded according to priority and gave trained people information to decide whether to continue.

Hamilton argued that software deserved the seriousness given to other engineering disciplines and should be treated as part of systems engineering. She later founded software companies focused on error prevention and reliability. Her career helped give software engineering professional weight at a time when the field was still taking shape.

She was also the first programmer hired for MIT’s Apollo project and its first woman programmer, according to MIT. NASA recognised her contributions with the Exceptional Space Act Award in 2003; President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. The familiar photograph of Hamilton beside an Apollo code printout captures the work’s scale, but not the team behind it.

Hamilton’s principles remain relevant as software affects transport, medicine, finance, public services and artificial-intelligence tools. Modern generative AI is not Apollo flight software: it can produce uncertain, plausible-sounding answers, while Apollo’s code was engineered for defined functions. NIST lists confabulation—confidently presented false output—among generative AI risks. The connection is not equivalence but the need for testing, clear limits and a plan for failure.

For AI agents that use digital tools, a polished response is not enough. Developers must consider what a system is allowed to do, how it signals uncertainty, what happens when a tool fails and when a person must approve an action. Safety is designed across software, hardware, procedures, operators and rules—not delivered by a single celebrated feature.

Hamilton’s work helped establish that software should be judged by how it behaves under pressure, not only by what it can do in a demonstration. Apollo’s engineering lesson was to build, test and improve a system for the unexpected.

MIT says Hamilton is survived by her daughter, son-in-law, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and siblings. A memorial service is planned for spring in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Her legacy endures in a question every high-stakes digital system must answer: when something goes wrong, what has the design prepared it to do next?

“I get asked a version of this question every day: why is Spotify in the business of selling software?,” he wrote in a post on Spotify’s engineering site. “The truth is, the Spotify you know and love is more than a great streaming service.

Though AI has made building such software faster, Spotify points out that this doesn’t necessarily mean it’s simpler — “the complexity, the cost and the operational surface area all grow with it,” Singer wrote.

The company’s foray into this space is not exactly new. As Spotify points out in its announcement of the new site, it’s been offering different products to the wider tech community since 2020 when it open sourced Backstage , a platform and framework for building customizable developer portals. It has also been selling its enterprise-focused software experimentation platform Confidence since 2023 and its enterprise software development platform Portal since 2024. Earlier this year, it began selling its developer tool for managing AI coding agents, Xirp . While many technology companies build their own internal systems to help their developers work more efficiently, it’s somewhat unusual to see a company like Spotify sell those tools to other businesses. Spotify’s SVP of Technology & Platform, Tyson Singer, acknowledged that the company’s move into this space has raised questions. “I get asked a version of this question every day: why is Spotify in the business of selling software?,” he wrote in a post on Spotify’s engineering site. “The truth is, the Spotify you know and love is more than a great streaming service. The company’s bet is that, despite AI’s advances, software development teams will still require certain core services, like those Spotify sells, which it says will be agent-ready. So far, it’s unclear how much revenue Spotify’s enterprise sales are generating, as the company hasn’t disclosed those figures in its financial reporting. That could potentially change as Spotify makes a more concerted push into the enterprise market, turning what was once a side business into a more formal operation. The technology website doesn’t include pricing; instead, companies can fill out a form to contact sales and discuss their needs. passages: Spotify has launched technology.spotify.com, a new website through which the company will offer external clients technology solutions developed for its own needs.

Spotify’s entry into this market did not begin with the new website.
In 2020, the company open-sourced Backstage, a platform and framework for building customizable developer portals.
Since 2023, Spotify has been selling Confidence, a platform for software experimentation, and since 2024, Portal, an enterprise development platform.
Earlier this year, the company also began selling Xirp, a tool for managing artificial intelligence agents that help write code.
Spotify does not disclose in its financial reporting what revenue it generates from selling enterprise software.
Spotify Senior Vice President of Technology and Platforms Tyson Singer noted that the company is often asked why a streaming service sells software.
According to him, hundreds of cross-functional teams work behind Spotify’s consumer app, releasing products and code every day.
Spotify believes that the development of AI is accelerating software creation while also increasing its complexity, costs and operational burden.
The company expects that development teams will continue to need foundational services, including solutions adapted to working with AI agents.

Police officers and first responders swarmed the Fred D Thompson Federal Building & Courthouse at 719 Church Street shortly at about 9:30 a.m. Officials say the suspect, described as a man in his 40s, pulled out a pistol and tried to fire, but the gun did not go off. He then pulled out a knife, and that’s when security discharged their firearm, officials said in a press conference. 10:49 a.m. - The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation will take the lead on investigating the shooting, officials said in a press conference. 10:46 a.m. - Police say the suspect “has ties to Nashville,” but they did not elaborate on the exact link. 10:43 a.m. - The suspect did not make it past the courthouse security checkpoint, a spokesperson said. The checkpoint is a critical measure to protect U.S. senators and other people entering the building. 10:42 a.m. - The suspect in the courthouse shooting was from out-of-state, according to MNPD. Officers and police K-9s searched the car and found nothing threatening, police said. 10:40 a.m. - Police say a courthouse security officer fired shots at the suspect after they entered the building armed with pistol. The suspect reportedly tried to discharge his gun, but it didn’t fire, according to MNPD. “This is the first time anything like this has happened at this courthouse,” the police spokesperson said. 10:37 a.m. - The suspect in the courthouse shooting has died after being transported to Vanderbilt University Medical Center, a Metro Nashville Police spokesperson said during a press conference. 10:34 a.m. - WSMV4 has reached out to the FBI, U.S. Marshals and the U.S. Attorneys Office for information on the shooting. 10:30 a.m. - Investigators are speaking with security at the courthouse to better understand the events leading up to the shooting. It remains unclear if anyone has been injured, but first responders have responded to the scene. 10:20 a.m. - WSMV crews share photos from outside the courthouse. Police have put up crime scene tape and cordoned off the area. 10:14 a.m. - The Metro Nashville Police Department says that because the shooting happened on federal property, federal authorities will be in charge of investigating. 10:10 a.m. - Nashville Public Library’s Main Library branch in downtown is being evacuated following a reported shooting at a nearby federal courthouse.
