The pilgrim journey, in short, involved fewer surprises. As AI becomes ever more pervasive and portable, pilgrims must now choose the degree to which they allow it to shape their journeys.

extraction.body: The two – Wayne E. Arnold and John A. Shultz – trained an AI companion on a smartphone to suit their travel needs, including translation. But they were also curious to see how AI would shape their pilgrimage experience. “Our hike became a test case for how pilgrimage might evolve in the digital age – not being diminished by AI, but reimagined through it,” they wrote later in the International Journal of Religious Tourism and Pilgrimage. AI tools are moving quickly into the realm of religion, including going on a pilgrimage. I have studied trails both ancient and modern and undertaken significant journeys on foot in the Middle East . What happens when an ancient and meaningful practice, often rooted in sacred texts, is affected by interaction with machines? From my perspective, AI is changing pilgrimages in ways that echo earlier disruptive technologies, from printing presses to steamships. Pilgrimages have always been an evolving practice, varying from place to place. In the Hebrew Bible, for example, God commands believers to go on pilgrimages in bare outlines: journeys to Jerusalem three times a year, coinciding with agricultural festivals , and highlighted by sacrifices at the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem. In the New Testament, Jesus and his disciples take part in those pilgrimages. Later, after the destruction of the Jewish Temple, Christians under Roman persecution quietly undertook spiritual journeys to places mentioned in the Gospels . By the medieval period, Christianity was the dominant religion of Europe, but long-distance travel was extremely difficult, and embarking upon a pilgrimage to Jerusalem was often regarded as a death sentence . Modern transportation transformed pilgrimages. Steamship travel in the 19th century and air travel in the 20th century all but erased the old overland Hajj routes and turned the long journey to Mecca into a much shorter experience, focused much more on visiting the sites and shrines at the heart of the pilgrimage than the journey itself. Even before transportation technologies made pilgrimages faster, information technologies made it easier for pilgrims to find the places they hoped to reach and to arrive at those places safely. Information technologies began shaping Christian pilgrimages quite early, with the first travel itineraries – written guides describing routes and holy places – appearing shortly after Christianity was legalized in fourth-century Rome . Early works by a female pilgrim named Egeria and an anonymous traveler called the “ Bordeaux Pilgrim ” functioned as guidebooks for travelers to the Holy Land and helped transform Christian pilgrimage from an informal practice into something more church-sanctioned and popular. Helena, the mother of the Byzantine emperor Constantine, aided this process by commissioning shrines such as the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem , where Christians still memorialize important events in Jesus’ life and ministry. In 1486, only a few decades after the invention of the printing press, Bernhard von Breydenback published his “ Peregrinatio in Terram Sanctam ,” the first widely available guide to Holy Land pilgrimage. Complete with woodcut maps and illustrations, the Latin guidebook was quickly translated into German, French, Dutch and Spanish. Von Breydenback’s book made it possible for aspiring pilgrims to follow his footsteps to Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Mount Sinai. But perhaps more importantly, for those who would never be able to make such a journey, the book exported the Holy Land to a curious European Christian audience through its illustrations and descriptive text. By 1500, it had been reprinted at least a dozen times . The printing press made pilgrimages an even more fascinating topic for Europeans than it previously had been. Journeys to places like Santiago de Compostela in Spain had already gained enormous popularity, starting in the ninth century C.E. The first printing of Geoffrey Chaucer’s “The Canterbury Tales” in the 15th century shows how pilgrimage was something people wanted to read about for fun. In that collection of stories, pilgrims are not holy travelers, but everyday people, often engaging in decidedly nonsacred behavior as they travel to a shrine in England . Indeed, during the Protestant Reformation, Martin Luther famously wrote that pilgrimage was no longer a sacred activity . “All pilgrimages should be done away with,” he said in 1520. “For there is no good in them, no commandment, but countless causes of sin and of contempt of God’s commandments.” But pilgrimages did not go away, nor did the profusion of information surrounding them. Each new information technology, from photography to film to the internet, changed how pilgrims experienced or shared their journeys. They streamlined planning processes, highlighted popular routes, eliminated uncertainties and often added safety and security to the journey. The earliest guidebooks had included descriptions of places, but with the march of modernity, travelers could see photos of sites, contact guides and reserve accommodations in advance, and share information in online forums. The pilgrim journey, in short, involved fewer surprises. Today, smartphone apps are available for many major pilgrimages, enabling greater communication with fellow travelers and sometimes adding layers of augmented reality to the experience. In online app stores, one can find Hajj apps that enable travelers to use their phone cameras to see pop-up information as they move around Mecca . And at least one online platform built for Jewish and Christian visitors to Israel uses AI to generate custom itineraries for potential pilgrims . Which brings me back to the Kumano Kodo in Japan, where contemplation is a key element of the traditional experience. In contrast to the busy and sometimes urbanized pilgrimage routes of Europe, or the crowded processions of the Hajj, the ancient path runs mostly through quiet forests. For Arnold and Shultz, carrying an AI companion did not interrupt the mood of the journey. As they write , “Rather than replacing reflection, it frequently initiated it, transforming moments of rest, curiosity, or uncertainty into opportunities for deeper engagement with the landscape.” As the hikers asked questions along the trail, their AI partner translated signs and offered historical information that enriched the pilgrims’ overall experience. “Unlike many of our previous hikes, where we typically bypassed the historical markers, we gained a more meaningful comprehension of the realities and the myths connected with the land we were traversing … we were moving through a curated poetic landscape that stretched centuries back, and more profoundly understanding its significance to Japanese culture.” In summary, Arnold and Shultz wrote that “AI, when deployed with instructions concerning personality and adaptability, can play a surprisingly human role in easing fatigue, boosting morale, and bringing levity to a journey. It was not just a tool or a translator but a conversational partner, one that made the lonely stretches of the trail less solitary.” What stayed with me was the qualifier in the quote above – “when deployed with instructions concerning personality and adaptability” – a reminder that travel-related technologies work best when used with care and intention. Hikers once had to remind themselves not to refer too often to guidebooks, lest they lose the real-life experience of being on the trail. Drivers have learned to be wary of instructions from mapping apps. As AI becomes ever more pervasive and portable, pilgrims must now choose the degree to which they allow it to shape their journeys. Treasury yields reduced risk appetite across financial markets.
Bitcoin fell 1.6% to just under $82,800 in the Asian morning as oil surged after a report indicated that the White House asked the Pentagon for attack options against Iran.

sources.title: Bitcoin breaks below $83,000 as oil jumps on Iran strike-plan report - CoinDesk
passages: The drop takes bitcoin below $83,000, the recent low that FxPro said on Tuesday would confirm sellers had taken control.
The firm said a break there could send bitcoin to $80,000 "fairly quickly."
Bitcoin fell 1.6% to just under $82,800 as of Thursday Asian morning hours.
Oil jumped on a report that the White House asked the Pentagon for strike options against Iran, pushing Treasury yields back toward their highest since 2002.
Bitcoin's last two losing days both came as oil climbed and yields rose.
XRP led the losses among the majors, down nearly 4% to about $1.42.
HYPE and SOL each fell more than 2%, and ZEC slipped less than 1%.
Besides the Iran report, a storm shut some U.S. oil output, and Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck two airports in Saudi Arabia, killing three people.
The jump in crude pushed the 10-year Treasury yield up two basis points to 5.31%.

It fell under that line, but is near $6 trillion in market cap now.
Nvidia sells the GPUs, networking equipment, and software that hyperscalers and developers need to build powerful models.
The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia.
Nvidia is currently the only company in the world valued at more than $5 trillion.
Apple ( AAPL +0.42% ) briefly followed Nvidia into $5 trillion territory before slipping back below that milestone.
Interestingly, Apple's AI opportunity looks different from Nvidia's.

The company doesn't need to dominate AI infrastructure because its enormous installed base of devices gives Apple something resembling a tollbooth through which developers can distribute AI-powered services.
There's another company sitting somewhere between these two models: Alphabet ( GOOGL -0.43% ) ( GOOG -0.43% ) .
That's why I think Alphabet can handily become the next $5 trillion company -- and potentially get there before the end of 2028.
Reaching a $5 trillion valuation requires its market capitalization to increase by only about 19%.
Wall Street's consensus estimates currently call for Alphabet to notch roughly $11.81 in earnings per share (EPS) this year, and expand that to $15 in 2027 and nearly $18 by 2028.
Alphabet stock currently trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 23.
This means Alphabet could reach $5 trillion by 2028 without requiring multiple expansion .
I think the competitive landscape is what makes Alphabet stock such a compelling long-term investment, though.

extraction.body: Nvidia ( NVDA -0.88% ) became the first company to cross the $5 trillion market cap threshold last year, powered by its position at the center of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure boom. It fell under that line, but is near $6 trillion in market cap now. Nvidia sells the GPUs, networking equipment, and software that hyperscalers and developers need to build powerful models. Apple ( AAPL +0.42% ) briefly followed Nvidia into $5 trillion territory before slipping back below that milestone. Interestingly, Apple's AI opportunity looks different from Nvidia's. The company doesn't need to dominate AI infrastructure because its enormous installed base of devices gives Apple something resembling a tollbooth through which developers can distribute AI-powered services. There's another company sitting somewhere between these two models: Alphabet ( GOOGL -0.43% ) ( GOOG -0.43% ) . Google owns AI infrastructure, develops frontier models, operates one of the world's largest cloud platforms, distributes AI to billions of users, and monetizes the technology across several businesses. That's why I think Alphabet can handily become the next $5 trillion company -- and potentially get there before the end of 2028. What makes Alphabet unusual is how it controls so many layers of the AI stack. Starting with infrastructure, Google spent years developing its own custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). Historically, these chips powered Google's internal workloads and those of cloud customers. However, Alphabet is now beginning to expand the opportunity by making TPUs available to select customers for deployment inside their own data centers. Alphabet is showing how AI isn't just confined to chatbots. Moving up the stack is Google Cloud and Gemini . The Gemini consumer app has 950 million monthly active users, while Gemini Enterprise is already being used by nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 . Moreover, the company is incorporating AI into search and advertising, where better recommendations and targeting translate directly into high-margin revenue. Meanwhile, Waymo is using AI to operate autonomous vehicles and has already scaled to hundreds of thousands of paid rides per week. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue soared 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. Even more impressive, the platform's backlog reached $514 billion . That backlog provides Alphabet with something growth investors love: visibility. Meanwhile, Gemini is proving that Google belongs in the same conversation as frontier models. Gemini models process roughly 22 billion API tokens per minute. As usage expands across Gemini Enterprise, Workspace, Search, and Google's consumer products, Alphabet has numerous opportunities to monetize AI research. Waymo provides another potential growth engine. While robotaxis aren't material to Alphabet's financial results yet, autonomous transportation could become a major commercial market -- and Alphabet already owns one of the most mature platforms. The bigger theme here is that Alphabet doesn't need each of its AI initiatives to become a blockbuster. Search can monetize AI through advertising while Gemini sells software and subscriptions. Cloud stands to benefit from accelerating infrastructure spend while TPUs monetize underlying hardware. Lastly, Waymo gives Alphabet an opportunity to commercialize AI in the physical world. Very few companies have this many shots on goal. Alphabet is currently worth $4.2 trillion. Reaching a $5 trillion valuation requires its market capitalization to increase by only about 19%. Wall Street's consensus estimates currently call for Alphabet to notch roughly $11.81 in earnings per share (EPS) this year, and expand that to $15 in 2027 and nearly $18 by 2028. Alphabet stock currently trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 23. GOOGL EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts Here's the interesting part: Multiplying the consensus 2028 earnings estimate of $18 per share by Alphabet's forward P/E of 23 produces a future share price of $414. This is about 20% higher than Alphabet's current stock price and would propel the company just above a market cap of $5 trillion. This means Alphabet could reach $5 trillion by 2028 without requiring multiple expansion . Of course, there are some important risks to note. Alphabet is spending enormous amounts of money building AI infrastructure. Competition from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft , and Amazon remains fierce. I think the competitive landscape is what makes Alphabet stock such a compelling long-term investment, though. Alphabet doesn't need Waymo to dominate transportation, Gemini to destroy ChatGPT, or TPUs to replace Nvidia's GPUs for this overall thesis to work out. passages: Nvidia ( NVDA -0.88% ) became the first company to cross the $5 trillion market cap threshold last year, powered by its position at the center of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure boom. It fell under that line, but is near $6 trillion in market cap now. Nvidia sells the GPUs, networking equipment, and software that hyperscalers and developers need to build powerful models.

Apple ( AAPL +0.42% ) briefly followed Nvidia into $5 trillion territory before slipping back below that milestone. Interestingly, Apple's AI opportunity looks different from Nvidia's. The company doesn't need to dominate AI infrastructure because its enormous installed base of devices gives Apple something resembling a tollbooth through which developers can distribute AI-powered services.

There's another company sitting somewhere between these two models: Alphabet ( GOOGL -0.43% ) ( GOOG -0.43% ) . Google owns AI infrastructure, develops frontier models, operates one of the world's largest cloud platforms, distributes AI to billions of users, and monetizes the technology across several businesses. That's why I think Alphabet can handily become the next $5 trillion company -- and potentially get there before the end of 2028.

What makes Alphabet unusual is how it controls so many layers of the AI stack. Starting with infrastructure, Google spent years developing its own custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). Historically, these chips powered Google's internal workloads and those of cloud customers. However, Alphabet is now beginning to expand the opportunity by making TPUs available to select customers for deployment inside their own data centers.

Alphabet is showing how AI isn't just confined to chatbots. Moving up the stack is Google Cloud and Gemini . The Gemini consumer app has 950 million monthly active users, while Gemini Enterprise is already being used by nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 .

Moreover, the company is incorporating AI into search and advertising, where better recommendations and targeting translate directly into high-margin revenue. Meanwhile, Waymo is using AI to operate autonomous vehicles and has already scaled to hundreds of thousands of paid rides per week.

During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue soared 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. Even more impressive, the platform's backlog reached $514 billion . That backlog provides Alphabet with something growth investors love: visibility.

Meanwhile, Gemini is proving that Google belongs in the same conversation as frontier models. Gemini models process roughly 22 billion API tokens per minute. As usage expands across Gemini Enterprise, Workspace, Search, and Google's consumer products, Alphabet has numerous opportunities to monetize AI research.

Waymo provides another potential growth engine. While robotaxis aren't material to Alphabet's financial results yet, autonomous transportation could become a major commercial market -- and Alphabet already owns one of the most mature platforms.

The bigger theme here is that Alphabet doesn't need each of its AI initiatives to become a blockbuster. Search can monetize AI through advertising while Gemini sells software and subscriptions. Cloud stands to benefit from accelerating infrastructure spend while TPUs monetize underlying hardware. Lastly, Waymo gives Alphabet an opportunity to commercialize AI in the physical world. Very few companies have this many shots on goal.

Alphabet is currently worth $4.2 trillion. Reaching a $5 trillion valuation requires its market capitalization to increase by only about 19%. Wall Street's consensus estimates currently call for Alphabet to notch roughly $11.81 in earnings per share (EPS) this year, and expand that to $15 in 2027 and nearly $18 by 2028. Alphabet stock currently trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 23.
GOOGL EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

Here's the interesting part: Multiplying the consensus 2028 earnings estimate of $18 per share by Alphabet's forward P/E of 23 produces a future share price of $414. This is about 20% higher than Alphabet's current stock price and would propel the company just above a market cap of $5 trillion. This means Alphabet could reach $5 trillion by 2028 without requiring multiple expansion .

Of course, there are some important risks to note. Alphabet is spending enormous amounts of money building AI infrastructure. Competition from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft , and Amazon remains fierce.

I think the competitive landscape is what makes Alphabet stock such a compelling long-term investment, though. Alphabet doesn't need Waymo to dominate transportation, Gemini to destroy ChatGPT, or TPUs to replace Nvidia's GPUs for this overall thesis to work out.

In the long run, Alphabet simply needs its vertically integrated AI businesses to keep compounding earnings. If the forecast above is any indication, analysts seem overwhelmingly bullish on Alphabet's ability to continue monetizing and profiting from its AI ambitions. And that makes sense.

It fell under that line, but is near $6 trillion in market cap now. Nvidia sells the GPUs, networking equipment, and software that hyperscalers and developers need to build powerful models. Apple ( AAPL +0.42% ) briefly followed Nvidia into $5 trillion territory before slipping back below that milestone. Interestingly, Apple's AI opportunity looks different from Nvidia's. The company doesn't need to dominate AI infrastructure because its enormous installed base of devices gives Apple something resembling a tollbooth through which developers can distribute AI-powered services. There's another company sitting somewhere between these two models: Alphabet ( GOOGL -0.43% ) ( GOOG -0.43% ) . Google owns AI infrastructure, develops frontier models, operates one of the world's largest cloud platforms, distributes AI to billions of users, and monetizes the technology across several businesses. That's why I think Alphabet can handily become the next $5 trillion company -- and potentially get there before the end of 2028. What makes Alphabet unusual is how it controls so many layers of the AI stack. Starting with infrastructure, Google spent years developing its own custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). Historically, these chips powered Google's internal workloads and those of cloud customers. However, Alphabet is now beginning to expand the opportunity by making TPUs available to select customers for deployment inside their own data centers. Alphabet is showing how AI isn't just confined to chatbots. Moving up the stack is Google Cloud and Gemini . The Gemini consumer app has 950 million monthly active users, while Gemini Enterprise is already being used by nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 . Moreover, the company is incorporating AI into search and advertising, where better recommendations and targeting translate directly into high-margin revenue. Meanwhile, Waymo is using AI to operate autonomous vehicles and has already scaled to hundreds of thousands of paid rides per week. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue soared 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. Even more impressive, the platform's backlog reached $514 billion . That backlog provides Alphabet with something growth investors love: visibility. Meanwhile, Gemini is proving that Google belongs in the same conversation as frontier models. Gemini models process roughly 22 billion API tokens per minute. As usage expands across Gemini Enterprise, Workspace, Search, and Google's consumer products, Alphabet has numerous opportunities to monetize AI research. Waymo provides another potential growth engine. While robotaxis aren't material to Alphabet's financial results yet, autonomous transportation could become a major commercial market -- and Alphabet already owns one of the most mature platforms. The bigger theme here is that Alphabet doesn't need each of its AI initiatives to become a blockbuster. Search can monetize AI through advertising while Gemini sells software and subscriptions. Cloud stands to benefit from accelerating infrastructure spend while TPUs monetize underlying hardware. Lastly, Waymo gives Alphabet an opportunity to commercialize AI in the physical world. Very few companies have this many shots on goal. Alphabet is currently worth $4.2 trillion. Reaching a $5 trillion valuation requires its market capitalization to increase by only about 19%. Wall Street's consensus estimates currently call for Alphabet to notch roughly $11.81 in earnings per share (EPS) this year, and expand that to $15 in 2027 and nearly $18 by 2028. Alphabet stock currently trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 23. GOOGL EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts Here's the interesting part: Multiplying the consensus 2028 earnings estimate of $18 per share by Alphabet's forward P/E of 23 produces a future share price of $414. This is about 20% higher than Alphabet's current stock price and would propel the company just above a market cap of $5 trillion. This means Alphabet could reach $5 trillion by 2028 without requiring multiple expansion . Of course, there are some important risks to note. Alphabet is spending enormous amounts of money building AI infrastructure. Competition from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft , and Amazon remains fierce. I think the competitive landscape is what makes Alphabet stock such a compelling long-term investment, though. Alphabet doesn't need Waymo to dominate transportation, Gemini to destroy ChatGPT, or TPUs to replace Nvidia's GPUs for this overall thesis to work out. In the long run, Alphabet simply needs its vertically integrated AI businesses to keep compounding earnings. If the forecast above is any indication, analysts seem overwhelmingly bullish on Alphabet's ability to continue monetizing and profiting from its AI ambitions. And that makes sense. When Bitcoin drops below significant clusters, many holders shift from profit to loss.
Those in profit can usually wait for a recovery, but those at a loss often sell to break even.
In the 24 hours leading up to October 8, Bitcoin briefly climbed back to about $84,300 before falling to $82,800, suggesting that holders sold off as the price approached their breakeven point.
In Bitfinex Alpha’s report on October 7 , they estimated that nearly 769,000 BTC, worth roughly $64 billion, were bought between $84,000 and $84,500—making this the largest cluster at any price.
At $84,000, 70% of all Bitcoin supply is in profit.
Bitcoin is more likely to face challenges below $84,000 than to quickly re-test the $87,722 level.
Spot buyers have remained absent during all three attempts to breach the yearly open, and ETF inflows are far below the $340 million per day linked to a recovery.
The upcoming release of September consumer price data on October 14 will be another pivotal moment for buyers.
If the report shows cooler inflation , traders may worry less about further rate hikes , which could improve market sentiment.
It has also dropped by 1.3% over the week and sits 34.2% below its all-time high of $126,080.
So, does spending a second day under $84,000 indicate that this support level has failed?
Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) attempted to break past its yearly open of $87,722 three times in just two weeks but failed each time.
Traders were closely watching for a breakout, but instead, sellers took control and pushed the price down.
Research from Bitfinex Alpha, the analysis team at the Bitfinex exchange, confirmed each attempt.
Whether $84,000 becomes a ceiling depends on one overlooked buyer group.
Futures contracts let traders speculate on price without exchanging physical coins.
Wall Street now controls more Bitcoin than Satoshi Nakamoto ever mined, yet the price keeps falling.

passages: Dogecoin sits 88% below its all-time high while Bitcoin closes in on a new record, and the math behind recovery reveals just how brutally different those two journeys actually are.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Dogecoin ( CRYPTO: DOGE ) is facing a steep uphill battle to return to its all-time high of $0.73, a peak it hit in May 2021. It needs to increase by about 735%, while Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) has a relatively easier climb ahead, needing only about 52% to break its previous record of $126,080. Although both cryptocurrencies have declined, Dogecoin holders face a recovery path roughly 14 times more challenging than Bitcoin holders.

Currently, Dogecoin trades at approximately $0.088 as of October 8, 2026. This represents a 3.6% drop in the last 24 hours and an 8.4% drop over the past week, putting it 88% below its peak price. Meanwhile, Bitcoin is trading at $82,969, down 34% from its record high. So, the question remains: can Dogecoin ever return to that $0.73 mark?

Many people assume that a price drop and the gain needed to recover are equal; however, that isn’t the case. The percentage gain needed to break even is always larger than the percentage drop. For instance, if a coin drops by 50%, it requires a 100% increase to return to its original price.

This gap becomes much more pronounced for coins that drop more. Bitcoin, down 34%, needs a 52% gain to recover, while Dogecoin’s 88% drop requires a staggering 735% gain. This is because Dogecoin’s current price is starting from a base that is about one-eighth of its previous high.

Additionally, Dogecoin miners continuously add new coins to the market. The network has no maximum supply, and miners generate 10,000 new DOGE for each block processed, resulting in roughly 5 billion DOGE entering circulation annually. This means buyers hoping to push Dogecoin back to $0.73 now have to absorb all the coins created since May 2021.
Chinnapong / iStock Editorial via Getty Images

A cryptocurrency’s market capitalization, or market cap, is calculated by multiplying its price by the number of coins in circulation. Currently, Dogecoin’s market cap is around $13.7 billion, with approximately 156 billion DOGE in circulation.

If Dogecoin were to reach $0.73 again, its market cap would soar to roughly $114 billion, making it worth more than eight times its current value. At that level, Dogecoin would surpass BNB’s $102 billion and XRP’s $89 billion market caps, positioning itself as the fourth-largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin, Ethereum, and the Tether stablecoin.

So far, buyers have shown little indication of reaching that level of investment. Large investors, often referred to as “whales,” added about 1.14 billion DOGE—valued at roughly $110 million—to their holdings in late September. Unfortunately, that amount only represents about 0.1% of the nearly $100 billion in new capital needed for Dogecoin to hit $0.73.

Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) give investors a straightforward way to invest in cryptocurrencies through their brokerage accounts, attracting larger investors to Bitcoin. In the third quarter of 2026 alone, US spot Bitcoin funds accumulated $6.3 billion , bringing total assets to around $111 billion as of October 6.

In stark contrast, US Dogecoin funds have only about $15 million combined in assets. Bitwise, a prominent player in the crypto space, even decided to shut down its Dogecoin ETF , with the final trading day set for October 14, less than a year after its launch.

Despite these challenges, Dogecoin has previously surged massively. In 2021, it rallied to $0.73, driven by retail traders, social media buzz, and celebrity endorsements. This kind of buying can appear suddenly and without warning.

Looking ahead, Dogecoin is unlikely to regain its all-time high of $0.73 in the near future. Bitcoin has a much easier road to a new record, needing only a 52% gain, while Dogecoin faces the daunting task of a 735% increase alongside an eightfold jump in market value as new coins continue to flow into the market.

For Dogecoin to have a chance, a few conditions may need to be met. Bitcoin might first need to surpass its $126,080 record , as retail interest in smaller coins often follows Bitcoin’s achievements. Furthermore, Dogecoin funds would need to expand significantly beyond their current $15 million, likely requiring the kind of social media-driven buying that propelled the 2021 surge. If Bitcoin hits a new high but Dogecoin funds remain stagnant, reaching $0.73 could slip further out of reach.

Dogecoin ( CRYPTO: DOGE ) is facing a steep uphill battle to return to its all-time high of $0.73, a peak it hit in May 2021. It needs to increase by about 735%, while Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) has a relatively easier climb ahead, needing only about 52% to break its previous record of $126,080. Although both cryptocurrencies have declined, Dogecoin holders face a recovery path roughly 14 times more challenging than Bitcoin holders.

Currently, Dogecoin trades at approximately $0.088 as of October 8, 2026. This represents a 3.6% drop in the last 24 hours and an 8.4% drop over the past week, putting it 88% below its peak price. Meanwhile, Bitcoin is trading at $82,969, down 34% from its record high. So, the question remains: can Dogecoin ever return to that $0.73 mark?

Many people assume that a price drop and the gain needed to recover are equal; however, that isn’t the case. The percentage gain needed to break even is always larger than the percentage drop. For instance, if a coin drops by 50%, it requires a 100% increase to return to its original price.

This gap becomes much more pronounced for coins that drop more. Bitcoin, down 34%, needs a 52% gain to recover, while Dogecoin’s 88% drop requires a staggering 735% gain. This is because Dogecoin’s current price is starting from a base that is about one-eighth of its previous high.

Additionally, Dogecoin miners continuously add new coins to the market. The network has no maximum supply, and miners generate 10,000 new DOGE for each block processed, resulting in roughly 5 billion DOGE entering circulation annually. This means buyers hoping to push Dogecoin back to $0.73 now have to absorb all the coins created since May 2021.
Chinnapong / iStock Editorial via Getty Images

A cryptocurrency’s market capitalization, or market cap, is calculated by multiplying its price by the number of coins in circulation. Currently, Dogecoin’s market cap is around $13.7 billion, with approximately 156 billion DOGE in circulation.

If Dogecoin were to reach $0.73 again, its market cap would soar to roughly $114 billion, making it worth more than eight times its current value. At that level, Dogecoin would surpass BNB’s $102 billion and XRP’s $89 billion market caps, positioning itself as the fourth-largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin, Ethereum, and the Tether stablecoin.

So far, buyers have shown little indication of reaching that level of investment. Large investors, often referred to as “whales,” added about 1.14 billion DOGE—valued at roughly $110 million—to their holdings in late September. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) give investors a straightforward way to invest in cryptocurrencies through their brokerage accounts, attracting larger investors to Bitcoin. In the third quarter of 2026 alone, US spot Bitcoin funds accumulated $6.3 billion , bringing total assets to around $111 billion as of October 6.

Despite these challenges, Dogecoin has previously surged massively. In 2021, it rallied to $0.73, driven by retail traders, social media buzz, and celebrity endorsements. This kind of buying can appear suddenly and without warning.

Bitcoin has a much easier road to a new record, needing only a 52% gain, while Dogecoin faces the daunting task of a 735% increase alongside an eightfold jump in market value as new coins continue to flow into the market.

Looking ahead, Dogecoin is unlikely to regain its all-time high of $0.73 in the near future.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.

When he's not writing or staring at charts, Sam's either: - Watching anime (currently convinced One Piece has better tokenomics than most altcoins) - At the gym sculpting himself into a Greek god - Listening to the music your mum warned you only bad boys listen to Connect: LinkedIn | Email | MacLabs Marketing
For Dogecoin to have a chance, a few conditions may need to be met.
Bitcoin might first need to surpass its $126,080 record , as retail interest in smaller coins often follows Bitcoin’s achievements.
Furthermore, Dogecoin funds would need to expand significantly beyond their current $15 million, likely requiring the kind of social media-driven buying that propelled the 2021 surge.
If Bitcoin hits a new high but Dogecoin funds remain stagnant, reaching $0.73 could slip further out of reach.
It needs to increase by about 735%, while Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) has a relatively easier climb ahead, needing only about 52% to break its previous record of $126,080.
Although both cryptocurrencies have declined, Dogecoin holders face a recovery path roughly 14 times more challenging than Bitcoin holders.
If Dogecoin were to reach $0.73 again, its market cap would soar to roughly $114 billion, making it worth more than eight times its current value.
At that level, Dogecoin would surpass BNB’s $102 billion and XRP’s $89 billion market caps, positioning itself as the fourth-largest cryptocurrency after Bitcoin, Ethereum, and the Tether stablecoin.
So far, buyers have shown little indication of reaching that level of investment.
Large investors, often referred to as “whales,” added about 1.14 billion DOGE—valued at roughly $110 million—to their holdings in late September.
The network has no maximum supply, and miners generate 10,000 new DOGE for each block processed, resulting in roughly 5 billion DOGE entering circulation annually.
This means buyers hoping to push Dogecoin back to $0.73 now have to absorb all the coins created since May 2021.
Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, and Solana are all climbing while Dogecoin slides in the opposite direction.

sources.title: China’s Manus raises over $500M in first funding round since split with Meta
passages: Chinese AI lab Manus’ parent company, Butterfly Effect, said on Thursday in a WeChat post that it has raised more than $500 million, the company’s first funding round since Meta was forced to call off its $2 billion acquisition of the startup.
The startup was said to be pulling in annual recurring revenue of over $100 million at the time.
Manus in August resumed independent operations following the end of the Meta deal, and said it was required to delete some user data as part of the split.
The company is also reported to be considering going public in Hong Kong, according to the report.
Boyu Capital and IDG Capital led the funding round, and existing shareholders Tencent, HSG (formerly known as Sequoia China), ZhenFund, and others also participated.
The company recently launched Manus 2.0 , which it says brings a new architecture with new products and capabilities built around a new harness.
It also introduced Cue, a stand-alone app that gives personal AI agents their own email addresses, phone numbers, digital wallets, and computers.
The app lets agents communicate, handle tasks across services, and make payments within limits set by the user.
In April, Chinese authorities ordered the AI startup to unwind the deal amid intensifying worries in China over losing AI talent and researchers to the West.
Manus makes AI products and agents similar to what companies like Cursor, Lovable, and Replit offer.
It offers a chatbot and vibe-coding tools to let users build apps and websites, create designs and presentations, generate video, and more.
Manus did not respond to TechCrunch’s questions about its valuation.

passages: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , Ben Longmier, CEO of Ambrosia Energy, and Bill Thayer, SVP and Head of Datacenter Solutions at Bloom Energy, come together on the Smart Systems Stage for a conversation on “ Where the AI Infrastructure Boom Is Creating Winners .”
Don’t forget about the 250+ speakers leading 200+ sessions.
The next major opportunity created by AI may not look like an AI company at all.
It could emerge in energy, data centers, cooling, grid technology, electrical equipment, infrastructure software, or entirely new categories that don’t yet have established names.

This industry stage session will examine which constraints are creating durable business opportunities, where new categories are beginning to emerge, and what founders can build as AI moves further into the physical world.
Infrastructure booms create opportunity, but the benefits are rarely distributed evenly.

integrityPreflight.title: Uber and China’s Pony.ai plan to launch robotaxis in London

sources.pageTitle: Uber and China's Pony.ai plan to launch robotaxis in London | TechCrunch

sources.title: Uber and China’s Pony.ai plan to launch robotaxis in London
passages: Uber and Chinese autonomous vehicle maker Pony.ai plan to launch a robotaxi service in London as part of an expanded partnership to bring driverless cars to Europe.
The relationship has since expanded to Europe, where it plans to deploy 2,000 robotaxis, starting with Croatia’s capital, Zagreb .
The announcement is the latest instance of Uber’s ambitious push into autonomous vehicle technology through a growing web of partnerships and investments.
In August 2026, the companies launched an autonomous ride-hailing service in Zagreb with a third partner, Verne.
Under that arrangement, Pony.ai supplies the autonomous driving system and the Arcfox Alpha T5 robotaxi, developed with Chinese automaker BAIC.
Verne, a startup set up by Rimac Group founder and CEO Mate Rimac, owns and operates the fleet, while Uber provides access to its vast ride-hailing network.
In February 2026, Wayve raised $1.2 billion in a funding round that saw investments from Microsoft, Nvidia, and Uber.
The total funding in that round could reach $1.5 billion thanks to an additional $300 million from Uber , contingent on Wayve deploying robotaxis, starting in London.
Uber has pursued this multi-partner strategy elsewhere.
In Dubai, for instance, it has struck separate deals with Baidu and WeRide to launch robotaxi services.

Pony.ai, meanwhile, has launched robotaxi services in four Chinese cities and secured partnerships with local transportation authorities as it works to expand into European and Middle Eastern markets, including Qatar.
Uber expects to offer AV trips in as many as 15 cities globally by the end of 2026, roughly split between U.S. and international markets.

The two companies said on Thursday that they would begin testing Pony.ai’s Gen-7 robotaxis in London in the coming weeks. The announcement is the latest instance of Uber’s ambitious push into autonomous vehicle technology through a growing web of partnerships and investments. The ride-hailing company has struck deals with more than 30 autonomous vehicle companies , including Pony.ai, over the past few years as it seeks to capture a share of the autonomous delivery and ride-hailing markets. Uber expects to offer AV trips in as many as 15 cities globally by the end of 2026, roughly split between U.S. and international markets. Uber and Pony.ai first partnered in May 2025, initially focusing on the Middle East . The relationship has since expanded to Europe, where it plans to deploy 2,000 robotaxis, starting with Croatia’s capital, Zagreb . Under that arrangement, Pony.ai supplies the autonomous driving system and the Arcfox Alpha T5 robotaxi, developed with Chinese automaker BAIC. Verne, a startup set up by Rimac Group founder and CEO Mate Rimac, owns and operates the fleet, while Uber provides access to its vast ride-hailing network. The London service will follow a similar model, although the companies have not said who will own and operate the fleet. Pony.ai won’t be Uber’s only robotaxi partner in London. extraction.body: Uber and Chinese autonomous vehicle maker Pony.ai plan to launch a robotaxi service in London as part of an expanded partnership to bring driverless cars to Europe. The two companies said on Thursday that they would begin testing Pony.ai’s Gen-7 robotaxis in London in the coming weeks. The announcement is the latest instance of Uber’s ambitious push into autonomous vehicle technology through a growing web of partnerships and investments. The ride-hailing company has struck deals with more than 30 autonomous vehicle companies , including Pony.ai, over the past few years as it seeks to capture a share of the autonomous delivery and ride-hailing markets. Uber expects to offer AV trips in as many as 15 cities globally by the end of 2026, roughly split between U.S. and international markets. Uber and Pony.ai first partnered in May 2025, initially focusing on the Middle East . The relationship has since expanded to Europe, where it plans to deploy 2,000 robotaxis, starting with Croatia’s capital, Zagreb . In August 2026, the companies launched an autonomous ride-hailing service in Zagreb with a third partner, Verne. Under that arrangement, Pony.ai supplies the autonomous driving system and the Arcfox Alpha T5 robotaxi, developed with Chinese automaker BAIC. Verne, a startup set up by Rimac Group founder and CEO Mate Rimac, owns and operates the fleet, while Uber provides access to its vast ride-hailing network. The London service will follow a similar model, although the companies have not said who will own and operate the fleet. Pony.ai won’t be Uber’s only robotaxi partner in London. The company has also partnered with and invested in British self-driving startup Wayve, and plans to launch a robotaxi service in the city. In February 2026, Wayve raised $1.2 billion in a funding round that saw investments from Microsoft, Nvidia, and Uber. The total funding in that round could reach $1.5 billion thanks to an additional $300 million from Uber , contingent on Wayve deploying robotaxis, starting in London. Uber has pursued this multi-partner strategy elsewhere. In Dubai, for instance, it has struck separate deals with Baidu and WeRide to launch robotaxi services. Pony.ai, meanwhile, has launched robotaxi services in four Chinese cities and secured partnerships with local transportation authorities as it works to expand into European and Middle Eastern markets, including Qatar. extraction.body: Of all the things Alexa Plus can do, I never expected it to make me cry. That pretty much sums up my year with Alexa Plus. One minute it will do something seriously impressive; the next, it acts like it doesn’t know who I am. [Image: Alexa Plus’s memories feature pulls images from your Alexa Photos albums. With Google’s rollout of Gemini for Home earlier this year, and rumors that Apple is finally bringing the full Apple Intelligence experience to Apple Home this month, now felt like a good moment to review Amazon’s progress. A year in, Alexa Plus is the best smart home assistant I’ve tested: It’s easy to talk to, handles routines and multistep commands, and helps in the kitchen. I use voice commands to control my smart home devices, help me with timers and recipes, add events to my calendar and groceries to my shopping list, and occasionally order something from Amazon. I use the screen-based devices as photo frames, for viewing camera feeds, and as touchscreen controllers for my smart home. Smart home control, routines, general queries, calendar management, and shopping are light-years ahead of pre-AI Alexa, mostly because the new Alexa understands me better. The big promise of LLM-powered voice assistants was the ability to say what you want without using stilted, precise nomenclature. When I started testing the new assistant, I ran into a litany of issues, from misunderstood commands to messed-up routines and very slow responses. I can say “Lock the front door, turn off the lights, turn down the thermostat, and tell the robot to clean downstairs,” and it happens promptly, without any back talk. Alexa is also much better at answering questions, especially in the kitchen. When I got home, I asked Alexa to help me cook it; the assistant pulled up the reformatted recipe, and we chatted back and forth easily while I cooked. I could ask, “What temperature should I preheat the oven?” and “How many ounces are 160 grams?” and it would remember we were discussing the recipe and give the right answer. Alexa still sometimes forgets what it’s doing, and getting back to the recipe can be tricky, but it’s the best voice-assistant cooking experience I’ve tested. --- What is Alexa Plus? Alexa Plus is Amazon’s revamped digital assistant powered by generative AI. You can access it by voice through Echo smart speakers and displays, Fire TV, and other Alexa-built-in devices. You can also access it in the Alexa app on smartphones and tablets and at Alexa.com. It is free to use on the web, in the app, and on Fire TV but requires an Amazon Prime membership or a $19.99-a-month subscription (in the US) to access on compatible Echo devices. Alexa Plus is available in the U.S. and Canada and is in early access in Mexico, the U.K., Italy, Spain, Germany, Austria, France, Brazil, Australia, and India. The original Alexa is still available for free on Echo devices. --- I’ve also found Alexa more useful for general knowledge, something it used to be terrible at, and calendar management has become more reliable, too. I can now email and upload documents and photos to Alexa Plus, and it can import events from them into my calendar. I uploaded 10 screenshots of sewing supplies from my daughter’s teacher to the Alexa app, and it found all the items and added them to my Amazon cart, saving me a lot of time. My favorite upgrade is creating Alexa smart home routines by voice. I think of something I want my home to do, tell Alexa, and it does it. I wanted the string lights on the porch to turn on when I walk outside; Alexa set up a routine using the motion sensor on the Ring camera. One night, my daughter came out of her bathroom complaining, “The lights kept shutting off.” I told Alexa to change the “Hallway bathroom light” routine to shut off after 30 minutes instead of 15, and it fixed it. Like many Alexa users, I had a lot of technical debt in my smart home, and as a reviewer, my Alexa app was a graveyard of zombie devices. To get Alexa Plus to work properly for me, I had to rebuild my smart home from scratch, deleting all my old Alexa skills and routines and killing dead and duplicate devices. And while Alexa has improved, the Alexa app has not. Adding, deleting, and moving multiple devices is still deeply painful, and the app experience is Alexa’s biggest flaw. What I really want is Alexa Plus to manage all that for me so I never have to touch the app. From setting up gadgets to troubleshooting issues, Alexa should be able to put devices in the right room and, if something isn’t working, figure it out. Every Show device is now a rotating billboard in my home for Amazon goods. Daniel Rausch, VP of Alexa & Echo at Amazon, tells me these ads are curated and designed to be relevant. “When it’s done well, an ad should show up with something useful at just the right moment,” he said.

extraction.body: Of all the things Alexa Plus can do, I never expected it to make me cry. That pretty much sums up my year with Alexa Plus. One minute it will do something seriously impressive; the next, it acts like it doesn’t know who I am. [Image: Alexa Plus’s memories feature pulls images from your Alexa Photos albums. With Google’s rollout of Gemini for Home earlier this year, and rumors that Apple is finally bringing the full Apple Intelligence experience to Apple Home this month, now felt like a good moment to review Amazon’s progress. A year in, Alexa Plus is the best smart home assistant I’ve tested: It’s easy to talk to, handles routines and multistep commands, and helps in the kitchen. I use voice commands to control my smart home devices, help me with timers and recipes, add events to my calendar and groceries to my shopping list, and occasionally order something from Amazon. I use the screen-based devices as photo frames, for viewing camera feeds, and as touchscreen controllers for my smart home. Smart home control, routines, general queries, calendar management, and shopping are light-years ahead of pre-AI Alexa, mostly because the new Alexa understands me better. The big promise of LLM-powered voice assistants was the ability to say what you want without using stilted, precise nomenclature. When I started testing the new assistant, I ran into a litany of issues, from misunderstood commands to messed-up routines and very slow responses. I can say “Lock the front door, turn off the lights, turn down the thermostat, and tell the robot to clean downstairs,” and it happens promptly, without any back talk. Alexa is also much better at answering questions, especially in the kitchen. When I got home, I asked Alexa to help me cook it; the assistant pulled up the reformatted recipe, and we chatted back and forth easily while I cooked. I could ask, “What temperature should I preheat the oven?” and “How many ounces are 160 grams?” and it would remember we were discussing the recipe and give the right answer. Alexa still sometimes forgets what it’s doing, and getting back to the recipe can be tricky, but it’s the best voice-assistant cooking experience I’ve tested. --- What is Alexa Plus? Alexa Plus is Amazon’s revamped digital assistant powered by generative AI. You can access it by voice through Echo smart speakers and displays, Fire TV, and other Alexa-built-in devices. You can also access it in the Alexa app on smartphones and tablets and at Alexa.com. It is free to use on the web, in the app, and on Fire TV but requires an Amazon Prime membership or a $19.99-a-month subscription (in the US) to access on compatible Echo devices. Alexa Plus is available in the U.S. and Canada and is in early access in Mexico, the U.K., Italy, Spain, Germany, Austria, France, Brazil, Australia, and India. The original Alexa is still available for free on Echo devices. --- I’ve also found Alexa more useful for general knowledge, something it used to be terrible at, and calendar management has become more reliable, too. I can now email and upload documents and photos to Alexa Plus, and it can import events from them into my calendar. I uploaded 10 screenshots of sewing supplies from my daughter’s teacher to the Alexa app, and it found all the items and added them to my Amazon cart, saving me a lot of time. My favorite upgrade is creating Alexa smart home routines by voice. I think of something I want my home to do, tell Alexa, and it does it. I wanted the string lights on the porch to turn on when I walk outside; Alexa set up a routine using the motion sensor on the Ring camera. One night, my daughter came out of her bathroom complaining, “The lights kept shutting off.” I told Alexa to change the “Hallway bathroom light” routine to shut off after 30 minutes instead of 15, and it fixed it. Like many Alexa users, I had a lot of technical debt in my smart home, and as a reviewer, my Alexa app was a graveyard of zombie devices. To get Alexa Plus to work properly for me, I had to rebuild my smart home from scratch, deleting all my old Alexa skills and routines and killing dead and duplicate devices. And while Alexa has improved, the Alexa app has not. Adding, deleting, and moving multiple devices is still deeply painful, and the app experience is Alexa’s biggest flaw. What I really want is Alexa Plus to manage all that for me so I never have to touch the app. From setting up gadgets to troubleshooting issues, Alexa should be able to put devices in the right room and, if something isn’t working, figure it out. Every Show device is now a rotating billboard in my home for Amazon goods. Daniel Rausch, VP of Alexa & Echo at Amazon, tells me these ads are curated and designed to be relevant. “When it’s done well, an ad should show up with something useful at just the right moment,” he said.

Meet Interface, a new $99 smart ring from AI and hardware startup Natura that’s designed for the era of AI agents. With a press of your finger, you can ask an AI agent to complete a task, capture thoughts, and get things done without reaching for your phone. And while AI is at the heart of Interface, the ring also doubles as a health tracker, as it monitors metrics like heart rate, HRV, sleep, and activity. The startup was founded by Carlo Edoardo Ferraris, who previously founded tech accessories company Rolling Square . After years of building consumer hardware, he became convinced that rapidly advancing AI needed a new kind of interface that lets people ask for what they want the way they’d ask a person. The idea behind Interface is to help people look up from their phones while getting everyday tasks done more quickly and naturally. At launch, the ring will connect with a range of AI agents and apps, including Meta’s Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, Claude, ChatGPT, and more. Pre-orders are expected to open next month, with shipping slated for December or January. The smart ring was not the company’s first product. Those were HumanPods, a pair of AI-enabled earbuds designed to let users interact with AI agents. But Natura believed it needed a new form factor built for the latest advances in voice technology. “Over time, we evolved to an understanding where you really want to have access to your agents 24/7,” Ferraris told TechCrunch in an interview. “You don’t want to have even one hour of your day where you cannot access them. And the form factor of the ring is perfect for this because it’s basically an extension of you. You can go shower with it; you can sleep with it. You never take it off.” The company says the use cases are endless. If you’re out for a run, you could ask the ring to start tracking your workout. When you wake up, you could ask what’s on your schedule for the day. If you’re in the shower and realize you’re out of shampoo, you could ask the ring to reorder it. If you’re falling asleep while watching TV, you could tell it to turn off the TV and set an alarm for the morning. After using it to record a meeting, you could ask it to send your notes from the discussion to a coworker. Responses from agents can be delivered through connected headphones, an iPhone Live Activity, or the NatureOS app. Plus, users who rely on multiple AI agents and apps can specify which one they want to handle a particular task. For example, they could ask Claude to write code, Instinct to book a reservation, and Grokbot to take care of something else. In addition to controlling AI agents, users can control their devices, including their computers. Ferraris says he believes that, ultimately, most of the things people do on their computers will be handled through AI agents. He sees the ring eventually replacing many tasks that currently require screens, from filling out forms and messaging in apps to finding files and drafting presentations, with simple voice requests to an AI agent. “Ultimately, the main interface between users and technology is going to be the ring,” Ferraris said. “So it’s not going to be immediate because even today, not everybody has a personal agent, but I think everybody is bound to have one. So in this first phase, we expect it’s going to be for the people that already have a personal agent, which is mostly people in tech. But eventually, I think within a year, more or less, most people will have a personal agent.” Although the ring will launch at $99, Natura plans to eventually raise the price. For now, the company wants to get the device into people’s hands, build usage, and create demand before doing so. After an initial three- to six-month free period, Natura plans to charge a $9 monthly subscription fee. The company says the ring’s manufacturing costs are comparable to those of products like the Oura Ring and Samsung Galaxy Ring because they use many of the same components. However, Natura plans to price its ring lower initially to reduce the barrier to entry and drive adoption. As for health tracking, the ring tracks heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, different sleep stages, daily movement and step count, and skin temperature over time. The company says the ring can last 6 to 12 days on a full charge, depending on usage, and takes 100 minutes to fully recharge. While the smart ring market is filled with health-focused offerings from companies like Oura, Ultrahuman, and RingConn, as well as AI-focused ones from companies like Pebble and Vocci, Ferraris believes Interface stands out by combining both worlds. “This ring that we’re about to launch is significantly different compared to any other ring out there today because we were able to combine not only the highest quality health tracking with the rest of the components that allow for agent communication and meeting recordings and external memory, but we were also able to do that with an incredibly long battery life, which is vital for a product like this, and in a size that is very, very small. The product itself is, from a hardware perspective, very different from anything else that’s out there.” Anthropic is giving startups a free year of Claude Team and $1,000 in credits Russell Brandom At 19, founder raises $11M for Ghost, maker of a $3,499 computer for personal AI Dominic-Madori Davis Trump unveils his new Super Intelligence Force Anthony Ha Amazon responds to data center backlash, says it no longer uses NDAs Anthony Ha OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’ Anthony Ha Meta wants your next gadget to be Muse-infused Kirsten Korosec

He sees the ring eventually replacing many tasks that currently require screens, from filling out forms and messaging in apps to finding files and drafting presentations, with simple voice requests to an AI agent.
